title: Getting water through lake ice
summary: A hole in lake ice gives liquid water for far less fuel than melting snow, but only from ice thick enough to stand on. Measure it, go with a partner, a rope and ice picks, and keep off the thin ice at inlets, outlets, springs and moving water. Cover the hole to keep it open overnight, and treat the water like any surface water.

materials.item: Foam life jacket or float suit
Ice picks, where you can grab them in a hurry
Ice chisel (spud bar) or hand auger
Cordless drill with a long 16 mm (5/8 in) wood auger bit, for measuring
Jug or small bucket on a cord or pole, for scooping

materials.qty: as many as the sled takes

materials.item: Foam board or a similar slab to cover the hole (a block of snow does the same job)

steps.text: Plan the trip for daylight, with a partner, and tell someone at home where you're going and when you'll be back (CRC ICE, LSS).
Put on a foam life jacket or float suit, ice picks where you can grab them, a whistle round your neck, and ice cleats; bring a rope, a long pole, a chisel or auger and a tape (MN DNR gear, CRC ICE).

Choose a spot away from inlets, outlets, springs, currents, pressure ridges and docks (Alberta ice, MN DNR formations), and away from toilets and waste (TC 21-3 keeps the snow and ice it melts for water away from latrines and garbage).
Walk out from the shore stabbing the chisel ahead, and stop often to drill and measure (MN DNR check, CRC ICE).
steps.warn: Turn back at less than 15 cm (6 in) of clear, hard ice, less than 30 cm (12 in) if it is white ice (double the clear-ice figure), or at any grey ice (CRC ICE, MN DNR thickness).

steps.text: At the spot, one of you drills while the other waits a safe distance back with the rope (CRC ICE).
Measure the ice in the hole with the tape hooked under its bottom edge (MN DNR check).
Scoop water with a jug or small bucket on a cord or pole, and keep your mitts dry.
steps.warn: Wet mitts and sleeves freeze fast at the hole. Change into dry ones at once and watch each other for white patches of frostbite.

steps.text: Fill the jugs on the sled, part-full if they may freeze on the way home.

Cover the hole with a block of snow or something similar to slow refreezing (TC 21-3); a slab of foam board is one thing that fits. Then mark it with a large branch or stick that shows from a distance, so nobody walks onto the cover or into the hole (Cottage Life, Criminal Code s 263).
Pull the sled back along your own tested track, keeping apart from each other.
Next trip, break the skim ice with the chisel and measure again before you trust the ice (MN DNR check, CRC ICE).

Treat the water before drinking. Boil it for at least 1 minute, 2 minutes above 2,000 m (HealthLinkBC 49b). If you cannot boil, use plain bleach with no scent or added cleaners: in cold water HealthLinkBC doubles the dose to 4 drops (0.2 mL) per litre of bleach with about 5.25% chlorine, and waits 1 to 2 hours (HealthLinkBC 49b).

notes:
## Why a hole beats a pot of snow
Liquid water under the ice costs no fuel to melt. The US Army's cold-weather handbook takes water from lakes and running streams where it can, to save time and fuel (TC 21-3); melting snow or ice for the same water uses up fuel and time (TC 21-3; see [Water from snow and ice](#guides/skill_water_from_snow)). The price is the ice itself. Falling through is most dangerous in the first minutes: cold water makes you gasp and hyperventilate, within about 10 minutes you lose the use of your fingers, arms and legs, and hypothermia takes about an hour (CSBC 1-10-1, LSS): read the [thin ice card](#browse/hazards/cold_water) before you go.

## How thick
| Ice | Least to walk on | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Walking or skiing in a small group | 15 cm (6 in) | CRC ICE |
| A larger group | 20 cm (8 in) | CRC ICE |
| One person (the Lifesaving Society's figure) | 10 cm (4 in) | LSS |
| White ice | double the clear-ice figure (30 cm if you start from 15) | MN DNR thickness |
| Grey ice | unsafe | CRC ICE |

Plan on the Red Cross's 15 cm of clear, hard ice, as the thin ice card does: at a water hole you stand in one spot, bent over the hole, next to a loaded sled. The Red Cross rates blue ice strongest and grey ice unsafe (CRC ICE). White ice, made when snow melts and refreezes, is only about half as strong as new clear ice (MN DNR thickness). Ice that has thawed and refrozen is weak until it freezes solid again (CRC ICE). Driving out is a different matter: 20–30 cm (8–12 in) for a car and 30–38 cm (12–15 in) for a full-size pickup (LSS). A sled with full jugs adds weight on top of the people, so use thicker ice than the minimum when you can.

## Measure, don't guess
- Go with someone. While one of you drills, the other stays a safe distance back; measure every few metres, because thickness changes across the ice (CRC ICE).
- Start at the shore and stop often as you go. On thin early- and late-season ice, stab the chisel ahead with each step (MN DNR check).
- Measure in the hole with a tape hooked under the bottom edge of the ice. Don't judge by how easily the chisel or drill went through: it is easy to overestimate (MN DNR check).
- A cordless drill with a long 16 mm (⅝ in) wood auger bit makes a measuring hole; MN DNR prefers a wood bit to a metal one because its flutes clear the chips (MN DNR check).
- Measure again on every trip. Thaws, snowfall and cold snaps all change it, and the Red Cross says to check ice regularly (CRC ICE).

## Where ice is thin
- **Inlets, outlets and springs.** Alberta warns about ice near stream inlets and outlets, and lists springs among the things that make thickness vary (Alberta ice). Open water at an inlet or spring looks like an easy water source; the ice round it can be thin, and Alberta says to avoid ice near open water (Alberta ice).
- **Moving water.** Ice formed over currents is often dangerous; on rivers the outside of a bend is weaker, because the faster current wears it from below (MN DNR ice safety). Avoid ice near moving water (LSS): about one third of ice-related deaths happen on flowing water (LSS). That is why this guide is about lakes and ponds, not rivers.
- **Pressure ridges** are always dangerous (MN DNR formations). Use caution near them (CRC ICE).
- **Gas holes**, often near stream inlets where plants rot, can hide under a skin of ice or snow (MN DNR formations).
- **Near logs, rocks, docks and bridges,** which soak up the sun (MN DNR formations), and near dark objects, air holes and rising mist (CRC ICE).
- **Under snow.** Snow insulates the ice so it grows slowly, and its weight lowers what the ice can carry (MN DNR formations). Heavy snow can push the ice down and hide slush (Alberta ice).
- **Near shore late in the season** (MN DNR formations).
- **Surface aerators.** A lake with a surface aerator running can have thin ice or open water (Alberta ice).

## The gear
- A foam life jacket or float suit. MN DNR calls it maybe the most important item for surviving a fall through, and prefers foam to inflatable in cold water (MN DNR gear).
- Ice picks where you can grab them, a whistle round your neck, a rope, and a long pole or branch to test the ice and to reach with (MN DNR gear, CRC ICE, LSS).
- Ice cleats prevent slips and falls on slick, new ice (MN DNR gear). Water slopped round a water hole freezes into a slick patch.
- An ice chisel or auger, and a tape measure. Auger blades and chisel edges cut: keep the auger's blade cover on between holes, keep mitts on when you handle the metal (see the [cold card](#browse/hazards/cold)), and insulate chisel and auger handles if you can (CCOHS cold work).
- A partner. The Lifesaving Society says never to go on the ice alone (LSS). The Red Cross adds: stay off the ice at night, and tell someone where you're going and when you'll be back (CRC ICE).

## Cutting and using the hole
- **The spot:** measured ice, away from inlets, springs, ridges and docks, and well away from where people relieve themselves or dump waste. TC 21-3 puts the snow and ice it melts for water upwind of camp and apart from latrines and garbage (TC 21-3).
- **Small is better.** An auger hole is wide enough for a small scoop on a cord, and easy to cover.
- **Keep your hands dry.** Scoop with a jug or small bucket tied to a cord or pole rather than reaching in. Wet mitts and sleeves at the hole freeze fast: change into dry ones at once, and watch each other's faces and fingers for frostbite (see the [cold card](#browse/hazards/cold)). The Red Cross warns against overexertion and long spells outside (CRC ICE).
- **Mark the hole** with a large branch or stick that shows from a distance, so nobody steps in it in the dark (Cottage Life).

## Keeping it open overnight
TC 21-3 covers a water hole with a block of snow, or something like it, to slow refreezing (TC 21-3). A slab of foam board under the snow follows the same idea; that version is this guide's suggestion, not the handbook's. Next trip, break the skim ice with the chisel and scoop it out, then measure the ice by the hole again before you trust it.

## Don't leave an open hole
A hole you walk away from is a trap for anyone who comes along later, children and dogs included, most of all after dark or under fresh snow. Canada's Criminal Code (s. 263) makes whoever makes an opening in ice that the public uses responsible for guarding it well enough that people can't fall in by accident, and for warning them it is there (Criminal Code s 263). So cover it, mark it with a tall branch (Cottage Life), and remember that a snow cover hides the hole: nobody should treat it as ice to stand on.

## Hauling it home
A litre of water weighs a kilogram, so a 20 L jug is 20 kg (44 lb). Pull jugs on a sled or toboggan instead of carrying them: see the [heavy loads card](#browse/hazards/heavy). The 15 cm figure is for a small group on foot (CRC ICE), so keep it to the two of you at the hole and spread out on the way back, walking in your own tested track. Fill jugs part-way if the trip is long and cold, so they don't split if they freeze (see [Keeping water liquid in winter](#guides/skill_water_in_winter)).

## Treat it
Treat water under the ice as untreated surface water. Clear it if it's cloudy, then boil it for at least 1 minute, 2 minutes above 2,000 m (HealthLinkBC 49b). If you can't boil, chlorinate it with plain bleach with no scent or added cleaners. It will be colder than 10 °C, so HealthLinkBC doubles the dose to 4 drops (0.2 mL) per litre of bleach with about 5.25% chlorine, and waits 1 to 2 hours (HealthLinkBC 49b). Check the strength on your bottle, and test old bleach first: see [Test how strong old bleach is](#guides/test_bleach_strength). Bleach kills bacteria and viruses but may not kill parasites such as Cryptosporidium and Giardia, which is why boiling is the better choice (CDC emergency, HealthLinkBC 49b). Sawyer says to replace a hollow-fibre filter if you suspect it froze after its first use, because freezing damage can't be reliably detected (Sawyer FAQ), so boil or chlorinate instead of trusting a filter that froze; see [Keeping water liquid in winter](#guides/skill_water_in_winter). Boiling and bleach do nothing for fuel or toxic chemicals (CDC emergency), so don't take water where fuel or chemicals may have got in.

## If someone goes through
Everything on the [thin ice card](#browse/hazards/cold_water) applies. In short: the first minute is for getting your breathing under control; after that you have about 10 minutes of useful movement to get out (LSS). Turn back the way you came, get your arms onto the ice (with picks, dig the points in), kick until you're flat and slide out on your stomach, then roll or crawl away without standing up (CRC ICE, LSS, MN DNR gear). The partner doesn't run to the hole, because that can mean two people in the water (MN DNR rescue). They stay back, lie down, reach with the pole or throw the rope, and tell them to kick while they pull (CRC ICE). If the person starts pulling you toward the hole, let go and try again (MN DNR rescue). Get them indoors, out of wet clothes and warmed gently (see the [cold card](#browse/hazards/cold)).
